title: Captive Crocodiles Don't Try to Go Home — But Wild Ones Do
summary:
Crocodiles are legendary for their homing instinct. Move one far from its capture site, and it will often travel vast distances to return — a behavior that has frustrated conservationists for decades. But a new study reveals a surprising twist: crocodiles raised in captivity may not try to go home at all.

The research took place in the Sundarbans mangrove forest in Bangladesh, one of the last strongholds for saltwater crocodiles. Heavy hunting for crocodile skins nearly wiped them out until the 1970s. Although the species has been legally protected since 1973, their numbers haven't recovered. The most recent survey estimates just 140 mature individuals remain.

Scientists fitted five mature saltwater crocodiles with satellite trackers. Three were captive-reared females that had spent 8 to 22 years in captivity. One was a local wild crocodile released where it was caught. The last, a wild crocodile named Jongra, was translocated (moved) about 132 kilometers from his original home.

The results were striking. None of the three captive-reared crocodiles showed any sign of returning to their breeding facility. Instead, they settled into small, well-defined areas and moved just like the local wild crocodile. "They are possibly able to adapt to their new environment seamlessly," said behavioral ecologist Ru Somaweera from Murdoch University.

Jongra, however, behaved very differently. Although he didn't make it back during the study, his movements clearly headed in that direction. He traveled farther each day than any other crocodile, covered an exceptionally large area, and even recorded single-day movements of more than 30 kilometers — all classic signs of homing behavior.

This contrast could change conservation strategies. Traditional reintroduction programs use hatchlings, but their survival rates are extremely low and they take years to reach reproductive maturity. If larger, captive-bred crocodiles can adapt successfully, they might offer a better solution for restoring declining populations.
why_it_matters: It shows how scientists revise their expectations when real evidence arrives, and how understanding animal behaviour can decide whether money spent saving an endangered species actually gives it a second chance.

background_read: Saltwater crocodiles are the largest living reptiles — the biggest can grow longer than a small car — and the Sundarbans mangrove forest, which stretches across Bangladesh and India, is one of their last strongholds.
The Sundarbans is the world's biggest mangrove forest, and it is also famous for its Bengal tigers.

Bangladesh made hunting crocodiles for their skins illegal in 1973, and the species is also covered by CITES — an international agreement that limits trade in threatened animals — yet the population still has not recovered.
Scientists often use satellite tracking to follow sharks, sea turtles and birds so they can see exactly where wild animals travel.

Releasing captive animals into the wild is called reintroduction, and Murdoch University in Australia, where the researcher Ru Somaweera works, is one of the places studying how well such programmes actually work.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — a new tool for conservation
perspectives.description: The study suggests captive-bred adult crocodiles may adapt to the wild far better than hatchlings, which could make reintroduction programmes faster and more successful for a species that has barely recovered since 1973.

Only five crocodiles were tracked, and three of them were females from the same breeding facility. Settling into an area does not prove an animal will survive, find food or breed, so the conclusion may be too broad.

The contrast between the captive-reared crocodiles and Jongra fits a wider pattern in wildlife science: what an animal does after release is shaped by the life it had before, not just by its species. Captivity may erase the urge to navigate home.

Longer tracking is needed to see whether the released females eventually breed, and whether Jongra finally completed his journey home. Those answers would decide whether managers switch from hatchlings to larger captive-bred animals.
